sections.title: Unit Vocabulary — Write each definition in your own words
Lesson 1: Measurement
objective: Identify SI base units and metric prefixes
concept: Chemistry is the study of matter and its changes. Matter can be described through its properties using two kinds of observations. Qualitative observations are descriptive and non-numerical (color, odor, texture). Quantitative observations are in the form of numbers and units (mass 5 g, temperature 371 K).

Every measurement has three parts: a number (magnitude), a unit (standard of comparison), and an indication of uncertainty. The SI system uses base units: meter (length), kilogram (mass), second (time), kelvin (temperature). Metric prefixes change the size of a unit by powers of ten: kilo (k, 1000×), centi (c, 1/100), milli (m, 1/1000), micro (µ, 1/1,000,000).

example.problem: Classify each observation as qualitative or quantitative: (a) the metal is silver-colored; (b) it melts at 371 K; (c) its density is 0.97 g/cm³.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Silver-colored describes appearance without numbers → qualitative.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: 371 K is a number with a unit → quantitative.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: 0.97 g/cm³ is a number with units → quantitative.

sections.title: Lesson 2: Significant Figures
objective: Round calculations to the correct number of sig figs
concept: Significant figures (sig figs) are the digits actually recorded by a measuring device. RULES FOR COUNTING SIG FIGS: (1) non-zero digits are always significant; (2) leading zeros are NOT significant — 0.003080 has 4 sig figs; (3) captive zeros between non-zeros ARE significant — 1005 has 4; (4) trailing zeros are significant only if a decimal point is present — 2500 has 2, 2500. has 4.

RULES FOR CALCULATIONS: For addition and subtraction, round to the fewest decimal places. For multiplication and division, round to the fewest significant figures. NEVER be more precise than the least precise measurement.

sections.title: Lesson 3: Density
objective: Calculate density using a numerical set-up
Solve for mass or volume given density
concept: Density is the amount of matter in a given amount of space — the ratio of mass to volume: density = mass ÷ volume. Density is an intensive property: a small piece and a large block of the same substance have the same density. Units are g/mL or g/cm³.
NUMERICAL SET-UP RULE: Always write the formula, substitute the numbers WITH units, and give the answer with units. Example: d = 74.6 g ÷ 27.6 cm³ = 2.70 g/cm³.

sections.title: Lesson 4: Scientific Notation
objective: Convert standard notation to scientific notation
Convert scientific notation to standard notation
concept: Scientific notation writes numbers as a decimal between 1 and 10 multiplied by a power of ten: N × 10^n. Converting from standard to scientific: move the decimal point so one non-zero digit is to the left; count the moves — left moves are positive exponents, right moves are negative.
Examples: 1,902,300,000 → 1.9023 × 10⁹ (decimal moved 9 places left). 0.0000025 → 2.5 × 10⁻⁶ (moved 6 places right).

sections.title: Lesson 5: Dimensional Analysis
concept: Dimensional analysis (unit conversion) uses conversion factors written as ratios to cancel unwanted units. A conversion factor is a number or ratio (in fraction form) used to convert from one unit to another. The given units cancel out, leaving the desired target units.
Example: 12.0 oz × (29.57 mL / 1 oz) = 355 mL — the oz units cancel, leaving mL. Always set up so the unit you want to get rid of is in the denominator.
